title: Daily X narrative digest — 2026-10-05

hits.name: levelsio
hits.text: Airbnb's entire rating scale is now 4.5 to 5.0 You can't make this up 😂
hits.hook: Airbnb's entire rating scale is now 4.5 to 5.0 You can't make this up 😂
hits.draft_en:
Airbnb's whole rating scale now lives between 4.5 and 5.0.

That is not a rating system. It is a pass/fail switch wearing five stars.

When every listing is a 4.8, the number stops carrying information. Guests stop trusting it. Hosts get punished for a 4.6 that just means fine.

If you run reviews in your product, check your distribution today. If the median is the max, your users already ignore it.

Fix the scale before you fix the UI.
hits.video_tip: 8-12s: a 1-to-5 slider squeezed into 4.5-5, caption your rating scale is a pass/fail switch.

hits.draft_en:
City states are running a talent heist on Europe and nobody is calling the police.

Better living. Easier work rules. Clear regulation. That is the whole pitch, and it keeps working.

Skilled people do not leave countries. They leave friction.

Your product works the same way. Every form, fee and wait is a reason your best users quietly move to the competitor next door.

List the three slowest steps in your signup. Kill one this week.
hits.video_tip: 10s: map with arrows from EU capitals to Dubai and Singapore, caption people leave friction, not countries.

hits.draft_en:
The limit on software used to be engineering. Now it is mostly imagination.

Greg's point: most software looks the same, so anything that looks different gets noticed, shared and remembered.

When AI can build the boring version in an afternoon, the boring version is worth nothing.

Spend your time on the version that makes someone say wait, what is that?

Take your current idea. Write the weirdest version of it in one sentence. Build that one first.
hits.video_tip: 10s: grid of identical gray app cards, one odd neon card pops, caption build the wait-what-is-that version.

hits.name: GREG ISENBERG
hits.text:
VIBE MANUFACTURING IS HERE

For the FIRST TIME in HISTORY, you can describe a physical product in one sentence and, a week later, hold it in your hands, cut from metal and built to your exact measurements.

That's VIBE MANUFACTURING, and it's about to do to physical products what vibe coding did to software. Maybe not today but over the next 24 months.

Vibe coding let people who had never written code build apps. Vibe manufacturing lets anyone make real things. You describe what you want. An AI turns it into a precise design file. A printer on your desk tests it overnight. A factory you found on a website quotes it in seconds and ships the parts in days. A $5 chip makes it smart, and your AI agent runs it.
hits.hook:

For the FIRST TIME in HISTORY, you can describe a physical product in one sentence and, a we
hits.draft_en:
Vibe manufacturing is the next vibe coding.

Describe a physical product in one sentence. AI turns it into a precise design file. A desktop printer tests it overnight. An online factory quotes in seconds and ships metal parts in days. A $5 chip makes it smart.

Greg gives it about 24 months to hit the mainstream.

The early winners will be people who already ship software with AI and now point the same loop at atoms.

Pick one small physical object you wish existed. Get it to a design file this week.
hits.video_tip: 12-15s: one-line prompt, CAD render, overnight print, metal part in hand, caption vibe manufacturing.

hits.draft_en:
Polymarket had Flavio Bolsonaro at 63% and Lula at 37% on election day in Brazil.

The interesting part is not the politics. A betting market became the headline number, and the sitting government banned prediction platforms back in April.

When a market price gets more attention than polls, people in power start treating it as a threat.

If you build in fintech or AI forecasting, that is your demand signal and your risk in one sentence.

Track one prediction market next to the news this week. Note which one moves first.
hits.video_tip: 10-12s: odds bar 63/37 then a BANNED stamp, caption the market became the headline.

Alex Finn's list for the last 30 days: Opus 5.5, Meta Muse, ChatGPT 6 Astra, Grok 4.7, GPT 6.1 sol, Sonnet 5.5, ChatGPT Dot.

Call it hype if you want. The practical fact is that good intelligence just got cheaper again, and agent launches are aimed at normal people now.

The gap between people who rebuilt their workflow this month and people who did not will be obvious by November.

Pick one task you do every week. Hand it to an agent before Friday.

hits.text: If you’re using Grok Bot, Dots, Muse, or Hermes, your agent is capable of WAY more than you think You’re probably only getting 1% power out of it The best strategy for getting way more done is the ‘reverse prompting loop’ Step 1: Give this reverse prompt: “Based on what you know about me and my work, what are 5 productive things you could do for me?” Step 2: Choose 1 of them Step 3: Do this over and over again until you have a ton of work done You’ll not only be ridiculously productive, you’ll also get tasks done you’ll never think your agent could do This becomes more powerful with the more data sources you have, especially the email connector I hate being in my email. Running this loop usually takes care of all my unread emails Try this out and let me know what you think!
hits.hook: If you’re using Grok Bot, Dots, Muse, or Hermes, your agent is capable of WAY more than you think You’re probably only g
hits.draft_en:
Your agent can do way more than you are asking it to.

Alex Finn's reverse prompting loop:
1. Ask: "Based on what you know about me and my work, what are 5 productive things you could do for me?"
2. Pick one.
3. Repeat until the list runs dry.

It works because the agent sees your connected data, so you do not have to invent the task. More connectors, especially email, means better suggestions.

Run the loop three times today and count how many tasks you would never have thought to delegate.
hits.video_tip: 10-14s: screen capture of the reverse prompt, five suggestions appear, one gets picked, loop arrow, caption let the agent pitch you.

hits.name: levelsio
hits.text: Another one!
hits.hook: Another one!
hits.draft_en:
Two words. 80k views.

"Another one!" works because the audience already knows the thesis. Pieter has been stacking the same few themes all weekend, so a two-word quote post reads like a fresh receipt.

That is the play: pick one thesis, then post every new piece of evidence as it shows up. Your followers fill in the argument.

You do not need a thread every time. You need a running theme.

Pick your thesis today. Post the next receipt in under ten words.
hits.video_tip: 8s: counter ticking up as screenshots stack, caption post the receipt, not the thread.

hits.text: I analyzed the range of ratings on booking sites and it's pretty crazy Airbnb goes just from 4.5 to 5 with a median of 5! But most others aren't better, they all range from about 4 to 5, and almost all have a median of 4.25, with not many scores outside of it! The best site in terms of honest ratings is actually Yelp, whatever they're doing it's working, it shows an actual normal distribution and ratings you can trust Hotelist itself is a normal distribution with median at 3.5, which was my goal, most stays are average/okay which I'd consider 3.5/5
hits.hook: I analyzed the range of ratings on booking sites and it's pretty crazy Airbnb goes just from 4.5 to 5 with a median of 5
hits.quote_note: quotes own post: Airbnb's entire rating scale is now 4.5 to 5.0 You can't make this up 😂
hits.draft_en:
Pieter analyzed rating ranges across booking sites.

Airbnb runs 4.5 to 5 with a median of 5. Most others sit between 4 and 5 with a median around 4.25. Yelp is the outlier with a real normal distribution. Hotelist aims for a 3.5 median on purpose, because most stays are just okay.

Honest ratings are a product feature. Inflated ones are a slow trust leak.

If you collect scores, plot the histogram today. If it looks like a wall, you are measuring politeness, not quality.

Design for an honest median and say so publicly.
hits.video_tip: 12s: four histograms side by side, Yelp's bell curve lights up, caption measure quality, not politeness.

hits.hook: Dear @1Password please remove the 0.5s animation everytime I unlock 😂
hits.draft_en:
Dear 1Password: please remove the 0.5 second unlock animation.

Tony's post cleared 50k views because every power user has felt it. Half a second, dozens of times a day, is a tax.

Animations feel like polish in a design review and like friction on day 300.

If your product has a moment users repeat daily, time it. Then cut it in half.

Add a setting to skip it, and announce that you did.
hits.video_tip: 8s: stopwatch over an unlock animation looping, caption polish on day 1, friction on day 300.

hits.draft_en:
Building an AI app? You host inference for margins. Then you support a few models. Then you need a router. Then people want evals, so you build tracing.

Yohei's point: that is how everyone ends up building the same thing.

The infra treadmill feels like progress and quietly eats your roadmap.

Before you build the router, ask if it is your product or just your plumbing.

Write down what only your app does. Buy everything else.

hits.draft_en:
Tony Dinh says it has been a long time since he caught a frontier model hallucinating.

Maybe they fixed it. Or maybe hallucinations just got rarer and harder to spot.

Rare errors are more dangerous than frequent ones, because you stop checking.

If you ship AI output to users, keep one verification step even when it feels unnecessary.

Add a source link or a check to your most used AI flow today.

When a post goes viral enough, the replies change tone.

Pieter quoted one about Airbnb ratings that reads like a PR agency wrote it. You can tell a comms team from a customer in one sentence.

Corporate voice is a tell on X now. It reads as damage control, and people screenshot it.

If your brand has to answer criticism, answer like a person: name the problem, give the number, say what changes.

Rewrite your last public reply without a single buzzword.

hits.hook: hotel bar staff laughing at 'ai tech bros' keeping my head way down
hits.draft_en:
Hotel bar staff laughing at AI tech bros. Ben kept his head down.

That is the outside view, and it matters. To most people, AI talk at the bar sounds like crypto talk in 2021.

The fix is not louder evangelism. It is showing one boring task AI did for you today.

Next time someone asks what you do, skip the jargon and give one concrete before and after.

Write that one-sentence example now so you have it ready.

hits.draft_en:
Nobody's personal agent runs on Opus 5.5 yet.

Ben's take: Opus was the goat in the early OpenClaw days, but the newest top model is not what people wire into their own agents.

People pick agent models on cost, speed and reliability, not benchmark headlines.

If you build agents, the best model on paper is rarely the one in production.

Run your agent on two models for a day. Keep the one that finishes more tasks per dollar.

outsiders.name: elvis
outsiders.text: 50K likes on this!? Most of what Karpthy has shared is things we have been doing for over a year. No surprises, as many replies are highlighting. But I still think this raises an interesting discussion. Is there a universal interface/langauge that allows more seamless communication between agents and humans? I believe there is. And I think that is what @karpathy is suggesting we think about. Right now, ideas are all scattered. As some of you know, I have been early on LLM Wikis, Artifacts, AI-generated visual explainers, dynamic interactives, etc. Over the past couple of months, I have been experimenting with a new universal interface for seamless human-agent collaboration. So I have a lot to share, but it's still too early, and I frankly haven't found the perfect solution. In short, my current optimal setup (see a simple snapshot attached) ties my high-level agent to highly flexible Notion-like pages that support embedding artifacts, text, videos, visual explainers, and just about anything an LLM can generate. And if it doesn't support it yet, I ask it to build it on the fly. It's crazy sometimes, the features it builds, but this is a co-evolved interface that satisfies both my agent's and my needs. The interface supports code review, note-taking, writing, research, prototyping, mock designing, and so on. In fact, I have now wired my agents to intelligently spit out these artifacts (for lack of a better word), depending on the task/instruction, instead of the default text responses, which are frankly overwhelming and hard to read at times. In other words, as I keep building this "universal interface," it feels less and less like I am chatting with an agent; I'm collaborating with it directly through the artifacts (through comments and suggestions). It allows me to move faster. I can consume and review faster. I am better organized. It feels like a language both the agent and I can speak fluently, so there is very little friction. Listen, this is all a personal experience. I don't think everyone will use interfaces like this. But it's been interesting to see Artifacts gain wide adoption, and now dots have Spaces that look a little like what I built here several months ago. More to share soon. [Quoting @karpathy Oct 1: We'll be spending a lot more time trying to understand the outputs of language models...]

virals.angle: A rating that is always 5 tells you nothing
virals.draft_en:
Airbnb's ratings now run 4.5 to 5.0. Median: 5.

Most booking sites sit between 4 and 5. Yelp is the rare one with a real bell curve. Hotelist aims for a 3.5 median on purpose.

When every score is high, scores stop meaning anything, and users go hunting for the truth in the one-star reviews.

This is coming for AI products too. Every agent reports that the task went great.

Pick one metric your users trust you on. Plot its distribution today. If it is a wall at the top, redesign it before they stop believing you.
virals.video_tip: 10-12s: histogram wall at 5 stars morphs into a bell curve, caption a rating that is always 5 tells you nothing.

virals.angle: Fix the room, not the agent
virals.draft_en:
Stop correcting your agent. Correct its environment.

The posts winning right now say the same thing three ways. pstack ships a /correct skill that turns repeated corrections into architecture fixes. CLAUDE.md files write the team rules down once. The reverse prompting loop lets the agent propose the work.

If you fix the same mistake twice, that is a missing rule, not a bad model.

Start a note called agent-rules. Every time you correct an agent this week, add one line. Load it into every run.
virals.video_tip: 10s: same red error pops three times, one line gets added to a rules file, error stops, caption fix the room, not the agent.

virals.angle: Your next user does not have a mouse
virals.inspired_by: @levelsio Nomads meetups MCP-ready (18k) + MCP Events spec (@jonas) + Agent-Reach (85k)
virals.draft_en:
There are two launch checklists now.

For humans: pages, categories, city pages, SEO.
For agents: an MCP server.

Nomads.com meetups shipped MCP-ready. The MCP Events spec lets one agent hire another and get the result back later. Agent-Reach gives coding agents eyes on X, Reddit and YouTube.

Agents are becoming customers. They do not click your buttons. They call your tools.

Pick the one action users do most in your product. Expose it as an MCP tool this week and post the demo.
virals.video_tip: 12s: split screen, a human clicking a page vs an agent calling a tool, both create the same item, caption your next user does not have a mouse.

virals.inspired_by: @karpathy 99% onboarded in under a year (160k) + @HNHughson no real use case (70k) + @AiWithSania LinkedIn prompts (311k)
virals.draft_en:
Karpathy: 99%+ of the people now paying attention to AI got onboarded in under a year.

That explains the whole timeline. Half the feed is posting 7 prompts for your LinkedIn. The other half says AI has no real use case. Both are beginners, one excited and one skeptical.

The opportunity is not more advanced content. It is clear, boring, useful first wins.

Write your next post for someone who started using AI last month. One task, one prompt, one result.

virals.angle: The plumbing is solved, the idea is not
virals.inspired_by: @yoheinakajima everyone builds the same thing (31k) + @gregisenberg imagination is the limit (310k) + vibe manufacturing (222k)
virals.draft_en:
Everyone is building the same AI app.

Yohei laid out the treadmill: host inference, support more models, build a router, add tracing. Greg says the limit on software is now imagination, not engineering, and that vibe manufacturing will do to physical products what vibe coding did to apps.

Put those together: the plumbing is commoditized. The weird idea is not.

Spend this week on the part of your product nobody else would think to build. Buy the router.
virals.video_tip: 10-12s: row of identical towers, one strange shape appears and the camera pushes in, caption the plumbing is solved, the idea is not.
